title: Deterministic communication versus monochromatic partition size
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal:
Determine the largest deterministic two-party communication complexity possible for a total Boolean function with a given bound on its monochromatic partition size, up to multiplicative constants.

For a total function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\) on finite nonempty sets, let \(D(f)\) be its minimum worst-case deterministic communication cost in bits. Let \(\chi(f)\) be the smallest number of pairwise disjoint monochromatic combinatorial rectangles whose union is all of \(X\times Y\). Define, for integers \(t\ge0\),
\[H(t)=\max\bigl\{D(f): X,Y\text{ finite and nonempty},\ f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\},\ \chi(f)\le2^t\bigr\}.\]
The target is the asymptotic order of \(H(t)\) as \(t\to\infty\), with matching upper and lower bounds up to constants independent of \(t\). This includes any nonconstant factors below the known quadratic upper bound; determining only the optimal power exponent does not meet this precision.
why: This tradeoff measures how much information a small monochromatic partition fails to capture about an executable communication protocol. Determining it sharply would delineate the power and limitations of a central combinatorial lower bound on deterministic communication, beyond knowing only its quadratic exponent.
status_note: The early Rao–Yehudayoff draft explicitly poses the gap question; its date has not been verified. The 2016 Ambainis–Kokainis–Kothari theorem resolves optimality of the quadratic exponent via a lower bound with exponent 2−o(1), but does not determine the finer constant-factor asymptotic rate required here. On 16 September 2026 the draft definitions/question and the 2016 theorem were read, and bounded later-work searches found no constant-factor matching result for the two-sided partition envelope. A checked August 2026 preprint on optimal unambiguous DNFs gives one-sided partition/cover and log-rank statements, which are different comparisons. This status is based on dated sources and a limited literature review, not an exhaustive current-openness certification.

importance.reason: A basic structural comparison in two-party communication complexity, connecting arbitrary rectangle partitions to realizable protocols and many lower-bound methods. The large exponent gap is resolved by the nearly quadratic separation; the retained target concerns the complete extremal growth rate and must not be presented as though that progress had not occurred.

sentences: Alice and Bob must compute a Boolean function of their separate inputs by exchanging bits.
A monochromatic partition divides its entire communication matrix into disjoint rectangles on which the output is constant.
The question asks for the greatest possible deterministic communication cost when the logarithm of that partition size is at most t.
A quadratic upper bound and nearly quadratic separations determine the optimal exponent, but do not by themselves settle all nonconstant factors.
This card asks for upper and lower bounds on the full worst-case rate that match up to multiplicative constants.

definitions:
Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know the entire function \(f\), the domains and the protocol before receiving their inputs. A deterministic protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies which party sends the next bit and gives a function from that party's private input to \(\{0,1\}\). The node itself encodes the preceding transcript, so each transmitted bit can depend on all previous messages as well as the sender's input. The bit determines the outgoing edge. Every leaf is labeled by an output bit, and on every input pair the reached leaf must be labeled \(f(x,y)\). In this convention both parties know the final output.

The cost of a protocol is the largest number of transmitted bits on any input pair, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum such cost among all correct protocols. Arbitrarily many rounds and either order of speaking are allowed. Local computation, local storage and the advance description of the function or protocol are free. There is no public or private randomness, no error, no nondeterministic witness and no quantum communication. Domains can be named \(\{1,\ldots,|X|\}\) and \(\{1,\ldots,|Y|\}\); transmitting an index uses its binary bits, not a unit-cost unbounded alphabet symbol.

A combinatorial rectangle is a nonempty set \(A\times B\) with \(A\subseteq X\) and \(B\subseteq Y\). The subsets can be arbitrary; they need not be intervals in a chosen row or column ordering. The rectangle is monochromatic for \(f\) when \(f\) is constant on it. A monochromatic partition is a finite collection of pairwise disjoint such rectangles that covers every input pair exactly once. Rectangles of both output colors are counted. The minimum size \(\chi(f)\) is a positive integer, and \(\chi(f)=1\) exactly for constant functions.

This is a partition of both the zero and one entries of the communication matrix. It is different from a cover that may overlap, from a partition of only the one entries, and from the minimum number of leaves in an actual protocol tree. An arbitrary monochromatic partition is not required to arise by successive row and column splits chosen by a communication protocol. The distinction between these combinatorial and protocol partitions is central to the question.

The parameter \(t\) is an integer bound on \(\lceil\log_2\chi(f)\rceil\); every logarithm here has base two. There is no bound on \(|X|\) or \(|Y|\) other than finiteness, and the maximum defining \(H(t)\) ranges over all their choices and all total Boolean functions. One may restrict to numbered finite sets to make this a set-indexed definition. Partial functions with unspecified or promised-away matrix entries are not included.

The universal upper bound \(D(f)=O((\log_2\chi(f))^2)\) for nonconstant functions shows that the set of integer costs in the definition of \(H(t)\) is bounded for each \(t\). It is nonempty because constant functions are allowed, and thus its maximum exists and is attained by at least one finite function. In particular \(H(0)=0\). No unique extremizing matrix is presumed.

An asymptotic answer supplies a positive comparison function \(g\) on the positive integers and constants \(c,C>0\) and \(t_0\ge1\) such that
\[c\,g(t)\le H(t)\le C\,g(t)\quad\text{for every integer }t\ge t_0.\]
The constants do not depend on \(t\), the matrix dimensions or the function. The upper bound must apply to every total Boolean function with \(\chi(f)\le2^t\). The lower bound must establish, for every sufficiently large \(t\), a finite total function with that partition-size bound and deterministic cost at least \(c g(t)\). No efficient algorithm for constructing the lower-bound examples or for finding an optimal protocol is imposed.

The target is the full worst-case rate up to constant factors. For instance, separating the measures by a power arbitrarily close to two establishes the optimal exponent against any fixed smaller power, but does not distinguish a quadratic rate from a quadratic rate divided by an unbounded slowly growing factor. Simply repeating the maximum that defines \(H\), or computing it for finitely many parameters, is not an asymptotic determination.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked determination of the asymptotic order of \(H(t)\), giving a comparison function and matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants for all sufficiently large integer \(t\). The proof must use arbitrary-round, deterministic, worst-case bit communication for total Boolean functions and the two-sided disjoint rectangle partition defined here. An upper bound for all functions and a lower-bound family must establish the same rate; a separation merely approaching the optimal exponent is insufficient if nonconstant factors remain unresolved. A result about overlapping covers, one-color partitions, randomized communication or partial functions does not by itself settle this target. No uniform efficient construction is required. The default absolute numerical tolerance does not apply to this asymptotic question.

source_formulation.text: Open Problem 1.12 cites a superlinear separation between deterministic communication and the logarithm of a monochromatic partition size, and asks for the best parameters in the quadratic protocol upper bound. This card retains the two-sided partition comparison explicitly named in that question and in the imported title.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open Problem 1.12; the worst-case tradeoff is written as H(t), with constant-factor asymptotic precision

context_blocks.text: A deterministic conversation identifies its input pair by following a sequence of decisions, each based on one participant’s knowledge. Every terminal transcript corresponds to a monochromatic rectangle, so a short protocol necessarily provides a small partition of the communication matrix.

The converse asks how much more communication is needed to turn a compact combinatorial description into an actual conversation. A partition may describe where every output occurs without providing either participant with a cheap way to determine which rectangle contains their private pair of inputs.

The standard bounds are \(\log_2\chi(f)\le D(f)\le O((\log_2\chi(f))^2)\) for nonconstant total functions. The upper theorem in the draft even allows overlapping monochromatic covers; disjoint partitions satisfy its hypothesis. The present target is specifically the partition variant in the source’s separation question.

The draft cites the 2015 separation of Göös, Pitassi and Watson. Ambainis, Kokainis and Kothari subsequently establish families with \(D(f)\ge(\log_2\chi(f))^{2-o(1)}\), showing that no fixed power below two can be a universal upper bound. This settles the power-exponent aspect of the earlier gap, but the theorem is described as nearly optimal and does not give a constant-factor determination of \(H(t)\).

The partition number is a structural lower bound on communication, rather than an algorithmic cost of finding the partition. Both parties may know the partition and still need a substantial conversation to locate their input. Computational hardness of discovering an optimal partition is therefore a different issue.

The inherited draft asks for the optimal gap without defining a comparison function. Writing the extremal envelope H(t) makes that quantitative target explicit and avoids replacing it by a single threshold assertion. The requested asymptotic precision retains slowly varying factors that an exponent-only formulation would discard.
